final.title: 9 Notes on Adjustments
final.stakes: Stakes: if this does not work or the viewer does nothing, practitioners keep thinking an adjustment means being pushed deeper. Some stay away from Mysore class because they fear hands-on help. Others accept help that is too strong and stop listening to their breath. Teachers keep adjusting without asking or noticing, and their students quietly leave after a few months.
final.why_care: Why care: right now a Bangkok office worker or a home practitioner in China either avoids hands-on help or cannot tell good hands from bad ones. A teacher may be asking why students stop coming. These 9 notes give both a simple test they can use tomorrow: light hands, the breath leads, the teacher asks every day, never force, and a teacher who notices.

slides.text: You think a teacher's hands should push you deeper. The best adjustments do less, so you do more.
slides.credit: 9 notes from 14 years teaching in Bangkok · swipe
slides.photo_hint: Wide, calm frame: teacher with one light hand on a student in a deep backbend or forward fold, with empty wall or floor for the big word. Faces at ease, nothing that looks like pressing down. Student's face not clear unless they have said yes to being posted.
slides.source: none (AYBKK has taught Ashtanga in Bangkok for 14 years, allowed fact; written as teaching years, not practice years)

slides.text: Light hands teach more than strong hands. A push moves you for one breath. A light touch shows you where to move, so you can do it alone.
slides.photo_hint: Close-ish shot of fingertips or an open palm resting on a student's back in a seated forward fold. The touch should look light.

slides.text: Your breath is the boss, not the teacher's hands. When the breath gets short or stuck, the hands come off. A deeper asana with a held breath is not progress.
slides.photo_hint: A twist (Marichyasana type) where the student's ribs and back are visible and the teacher's hand rests on the back or shoulder, student calm.

slides.text: A good teacher asks every day, because last week's yes is not today's yes. Even students of many years get asked. You can say no any day, no reason needed.
slides.photo_hint: Teacher kneeling or leaning in beside the student just before or at the first moment of contact, ideally a hand hovering or the teacher speaking to the student.

slides.text: A good adjustment draws a body map, not a shape. The hand comes the moment you move: which part, which way, what for. We call it drawing the cortical map.
slides.photo_hint: Hand placed on one clear spot (shoulder blade, hip or lower ribs) during a handstand, twist or backbend, so the eye sees 'which part'.
slides.source: none (teacher's own method name 'drawing the cortical map', allowed fact; used as a teaching picture, not a study claim)

slides.text: In drop backs, most of the help is for fear, not for flexibility. A steady hand helps you keep breathing. Then it does a little less each week.
slides.photo_hint: Assisted drop back: teacher's hands steady at the student's waist or lower back, student arching back. Must be a drop back photo. Hands should look steady and light, not pulling.

slides.text: No hands can make you ready. In Mysore class, the teacher gives the next asana when you are ready. Pushing to get there faster only slows you down.
slides.photo_hint: Teacher guiding a student into an asana with light hands, or standing close and watching; other students practising their own sequence in the background shows Mysore class.
slides.source: none (Mysore class method, the teacher gives the next asana when the student is ready, is an allowed fact)

slides.text: Experts need adjustments too, not only beginners. Skilled gymnasts and ballet dancers still need a coach's hands now and then. My wife has practised for years. She asked me for one.
slides.photo_hint: An experienced student in an advanced asana (handstand or deep backbend) with the teacher helping. Use a photo of his wife only with her yes. With any other student, cut the last two sentences ('My wife has practised for years. She asked me for one.'), so no viewer thinks that student is his wife.
slides.source: none (Boonchu's view of 4 Oct: even very skilled people need knowledgeable hands now and then, like gymnasts and ballet dancers; his wife, an experienced practitioner, asked him for an adjustment. Both are allowed facts.)

slides.text: Without trust, even a good adjustment feels like a push. You relax only when you know the hands stop the moment you say stop. That takes weeks, not one class.
slides.photo_hint: Student clearly relaxed (soft face, long body) in a forward fold or backbend with the teacher's steady hands. It should look calm and trusting.

slides.text: The first adjustment is to notice, and it needs no hands. Who came in tired? Who is missing this week? Noticing is why students stay for years.
slides.photo_hint: Teacher adjusting one student while looking across the room, or a hand on a shoulder with the room visible behind. A frame that shows attention more than force.
slides.source: none (AYBKK promise: a teacher who notices when you are gone, allowed fact)

final.caption:
The best adjustment does less than you think.

9 notes from 14 years of teaching Ashtanga in Bangkok. Light hands. The breath leads. A good teacher asks every day, and anyone can say no.

Teachers, the last note is why students stay for years.

Which one would you argue with?

#aybkk #ashtanga #ashtangabangkok #boonchutanti #mysorestyle
final.notes:
Boonchu, please check these before posting:
1) Slide 7 names your wife and is in your own voice ("My wife has practised for years. She asked me for one."). You told this story in your 4 Oct talking Reel. Is it OK on a carousel? It is the only "I/me" line; slide 4 says "we". If you say no, or if the photo is not of her, cut the last two sentences. The slide then stays at 20 words. Please do not swap in a different story, because any new story would need checking first.
2) Slide 7, line 2 ("Skilled gymnasts and ballet dancers still need a coach's hands now and then") is your 4 Oct view, not a study. Please confirm it.
3) Please confirm these as YOUR OPINIONS (they are written as your views): the best adjustments do less, so you do more (cover); light hands teach more than strong hands (1); in drop backs most of the help is for fear, not flexibility (5); pushing to get there faster only slows you down (6); noticing is why students stay for years (9).
4) Please confirm these as HOW AYBKK TEACHES. They are stated as house practice under the AYBKK MYSORE NOTES label: the hands come off when the breath gets short or stuck (2); a good teacher asks every day, even students of many years (3); the steady hand in drop backs does a little less each week (5); the hands stop the moment the student says stop, and trust takes weeks (8). The caption also says "A good teacher asks every day".
5) Slide 4 uses your method name "drawing the cortical map", so "function over shape" is left out of the whole carousel (one name only). "Body map" is a teaching picture, not a science claim. Please confirm the line "The hand comes the moment you move: which part, which way, what for" matches how you explain it.
6) No outside facts, studies, numbers or quotes are used. Every inner credit is the AYBKK MYSORE NOTES series label, and nothing is quoted as your words. The cover credit now says "14 years teaching in Bangkok", so it cannot be read as practice years (you have practised since 2008).
7) Photos: slide 5 needs a drop back photo. This carousel is about consent, so only post a student's clear face if that student has said yes to being posted while being adjusted. Until you confirm each student's yes, use frames where the student's face is not clear (from behind, turned away or far), the same rule we use for Google posts. Pick frames where the hands look light, not pressing.
8) Comments on adjustments and consent can get heated (Carne's earlier research). Reply short and kind, and do not argue about other teachers or styles.
9) Keyword test: there is no ask on the slides. The goal is 180K, so the caption ends with a question and has no "comment aybkk". No website and no link in bio.

issues.problem: The credit '9 notes from 14 years in Bangkok · swipe' leaves out 'teaching'. Plato's notebook (4 Oct, owner rule) says to always write 'teaching in Bangkok, 14 years' so it is not read as practice years, which would clash with practising since 2008. As written, it can read as Boonchu has lived or practised in Bangkok for 14 years. The caption already gets this right.
issues.fix: Change the credit to: '9 notes from 14 years teaching in Bangkok · swipe'

issues.problem: Two problems. (1) The fallback in note 1, 'A long-time student asked for one last month', is an invented fact. It is not in the allowed facts and no date is checked. (2) The slide says 'Boonchu's wife ... asked him for one' over a photo of a teacher adjusting a student. If the photo shows someone other than his wife, viewers will think that student is his wife. That is a privacy and consent problem for both women.
issues.fix: Rewrite note 1 to say: 'Is it OK on a carousel? If not, cut the last sentence (the slide stays at 20 words).' Add to the photo hint: 'Use a photo of his wife only with her yes. With any other student, cut the last sentence.'

issues.problem: 'A steady hand says you are safe' reads as a safety promise about drop backs, and assisted drop backs can still go wrong. Under the SAFETY rule the slides cannot promise outcomes.
issues.fix: Change it to: 'A steady hand helps you feel safe.' (same word count, 28 words)

issues.problem: It is not clear who asks. The cover and slides 1, 2 and 4 talk to the student ('your breath'). Slide 3 then tells a teacher 'Ask every day ... students you have taught for years', and a student reading it may think they are the one who must ask. 'Ask every day' under the AYBKK MYSORE NOTES label also reads as a stated AYBKK habit, and Boonchu has not confirmed it.
issues.fix: Change it to: 'A good teacher asks every day, because last week's yes is not today's yes. This goes for long-time students too. Anyone can say no, any day, with no reason.' (28 words, ASK is still in sentence 1). Then add slide 3 to note 3 for Boonchu to confirm.

issues.problem: 'they know you will stop' suddenly talks to the teacher, while the slides around it talk to the student. This is the same voice switch as slide 3 and is small, but it blurs who the slide is for.
issues.fix: Change it to: 'Students relax only when they know the teacher will stop the moment they say stop.' (slide becomes 31 words, still within 32)

issues.problem: Note 3 asks Boonchu to confirm only slides 1, 5 and 9 as his views. Three more slides state house practice as fact under the AYBKK series label, and none of them is in the allowed facts: slide 2 ('the hands come off' when the breath is short), slide 3 (asking every day) and slide 8 ('takes weeks').
issues.fix: Add to note 3: 'and these as how AYBKK teaches: hands come off when the breath gets short (2); the teacher asks every day (3); trust takes weeks (8).'

issues.problem: Note 5 asks for consent but does not say what to do until consent is confirmed. Plato's notebook says student consent to post faces is NOT confirmed, and it already uses a rule for that case: clear faces only for teachers, students from behind or turned away. On a carousel about consent, posting clear student faces without a confirmed yes is a real risk.
issues.fix: Add to note 5: 'Until you confirm each student's yes, use frames where the student's face is not clear (from behind, turned away or far), the same rule we use for Google posts.'

issues.problem: Someone who tried yoga twice may not know that 'adjustment' means the teacher's hands-on help. They might think of a chiropractor. So the cover does not say in one second what this is about. The flip ('do less, so you do more') works, but it only lands once you know whose hands we mean.
issues.fix: Big word LESS. Text: 'You think a teacher's hands should push you deeper. The best adjustments do less, so you do more.' (18 words). Keep the credit '9 notes from 14 years in Bangkok · swipe'.

issues.problem: Who 'you' is changes here. On slides 1, 2, 4 and 5, 'you' is the student. On this slide, 'you' is the teacher ('students you have taught for years'). 'Ask every day' reads like an order to the viewer, and a student cannot tell who is supposed to ask. 'With no reason' is also awkward.
issues.fix: Big word ASK. Text: 'A good teacher asks every day, because last week's yes is not today's yes. Even after years together, the teacher still asks. You can say no any day, no reason needed.' (31 words)

issues.problem: 'Cortical' and 'a map in your brain' are not 10-year-old English, and they read like a brain-science claim with no source. Sentence 2 ('It comes the moment you move: which part, which way, what for') is vague: what is 'it'? It also repeats slide 1 ('shows you where to move'), so the two slides blur together.
issues.fix: Big word MAP. Text: 'A good adjustment gives your body a map, not a shape. You learn which part works, not just how the asana looks. We call this drawing the cortical map.' (29 words). This keeps Boonchu's method name as the last line only, and it no longer repeats slide 1.

issues.problem: 'A steady hand says you are safe' is a safety promise, and it sits on the riskiest asana in the set (drop backs). The SAFETY rule says the breath leads and we make no promises. Tie the steady hand to the breath instead.
issues.fix: Big word FEAR. Text: 'In drop backs, most of the help is for fear, not for flexibility. A steady hand helps you keep breathing. Then it does a little less each week.' (28 words)

issues.problem: This is the weakest slide. Sentence 1 is soft ('Hands can help you feel an asana, but...'), so it fails 'says who?'. 'Ready' is used twice. The reader cannot tell who decides when you are ready. 'Forcing it is never the shortcut' sounds AI-written and hints that a shortcut exists. It also repeats slide 2 ('a deeper asana ... is not progress').
issues.fix: Big word READY. Text: 'No hands can make you ready. In Mysore class, the teacher gives the next asana when your body is ready. Pushing to get there faster only slows you down.' (29 words). Add 'pushing only slows you down' to note 3, the opinions Boonchu must confirm.

issues.problem: 'Boonchu's wife ... asked him for one' is in the third person, so on his own account it reads like a press release and sounds AI-written. 'Skilled people need good hands now and then' is vague. In the notes, the backup line ('A long-time student asked for one last month') makes up a time ('last month') that nobody checked.
issues.fix: Big word EXPERTS. Text: 'Experts need adjustments too, not only beginners. Top gymnasts and ballet dancers still train with a coach's hands. My wife has practised for years, and she asked me for one.' (30 words). If Boonchu does not want his wife on the slide, the last line becomes 'A student of many years asked me for one.' Do not add 'last month'.

issues.problem: The same switch in who 'you' is: 'Students relax only when they know you will stop' speaks to teachers. The main reader is a practitioner, and they cannot see themselves in it, so it makes them want to swipe less.
issues.fix: Big word TRUST. Text: 'Without trust, even a good adjustment feels like a push. You relax only when you know the hands stop the moment you say stop. That takes weeks, not one class.' (30 words)
